title: Memory hierarchy and caches
subtitle: Fast memory is small, big memory is slow — a cache makes the big slow one look fast by remembering what you just used.

hier.title: The hierarchy
hier.body: No memory is fast, large and cheap at once, so computers stack them: registers (sub-ns, bytes), cache (ns, KB–MB), main memory (≈100 ns, GB), disk/SSD (µs–ms, TB). It works because of locality: temporal (what you used you will use again) and spatial (what is near what you used will be used). The hierarchy moves data in blocks so neighbours come along.

mapping.title: Mapping: where may a block go?
mapping.body:
A block of memory can be placed in: exactly one line (direct-mapped: cheap, but blocks that map to the same line keep evicting each other — conflict misses); any line (fully associative: flexible, expensive to search); or any line within one set (set-associative, e.g. 2-way: the usual compromise). An address splits into tag | index | offset; the index picks the set, the tag is compared with each line in it, the offset picks the byte.

Same 5 addresses 0 8 0 6 8 into a 4-line cache: direct-mapped gets 5 misses, 2-way 4, fully associative 3.
mapping.steps: A 32-bit address, 4 KB direct-mapped cache with 16-byte blocks. Offset bits = log₂16 = 4. Lines = 4096/16 = 256 → index bits = 8. Tag = 32 − 8 − 4 = 20 bits.

policy.title: Replacement and write policies
policy.body: When a set is full, replacement picks a victim: LRU (least recently used), FIFO, or random. On a write: write-through updates memory every time (simple, slow; often with a write buffer); write-back marks the line dirty and writes memory only on eviction (fast; complicated). On a write miss: write-allocate loads the block first, no-write-allocate writes straight to memory.

amat.title: Average memory access time
amat.body: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. With a 1-cycle hit, 100-cycle penalty and the fully associative run above (40% hits) AMAT is 61 cycles — a cache with a 90% hit rate would give 1 + 0.1 × 100 = 11. Multi-level caches nest the formula: the L1 miss penalty is the L2 access time.

ext.title: Semiconductor and external memory
ext.body: SRAM (flip-flops) is fast and used for caches; DRAM (a capacitor plus transistor, refreshed constantly) is denser and used for main memory, in DDR DIMM/SODIMM modules. ROM/flash hold firmware. Externally: magnetic disk, SSD, optical and tape; RAID levels 1–5 add redundancy (see the OS course for a worked RAID 5 parity example).

summary.title: Summary
summary.body:
• Locality makes a small fast memory effective.
  • Direct, set-associative and fully associative trade cost against conflict misses.
  • AMAT = hit + miss rate × penalty.
